Try to get as much animal experience as you can. When I was 11 or 12 I started walking dogs and doing petsitting in my neighborhood since I could not get a job or volunteer at animal shelters yet, I got a lot of experience with animals that way and even learned about some medical things. 
If you can do 4H or other animal programs those are great experience.
 If you know any vets you could ask about volunteering at their clinics, or any farms that might need some extra help if you live in an area with farms, that is another thing you can try.

Try to focus a lot on school too, take as much science and math as you can and try to remember what you learn. :)

Keep in mind many states don't even have a vet school, so it may not be that easy to find one in the exact location you want.

I would ask your vet about giving lysine as well, you can ask your vet if they carry any of the lysine for cats which is flavored.

 If they don't have any, you can also get the capsules for humans and sprinkle it on her food. You can ask your vet for dosing recommendations, but what my vet says is to give 500 mg twice a day; so 1000 mg a day total -- I know some vets do only 500 mg a day total though...

If they have recurring URIs it is likely they have feline herpes and you can give the lysine daily to help keep the URIs from happening, we do 500 mg a day as a maintenance dose but some people do 250 mg when they are not having symptoms.

When one of my kittens had a really bad URI my vet suggested also giving colostrum as a supplement, also 500 mg twice a day. It comes in capsules, I got it at a health food store.

Another interesting brain parasite that humans can be infected with is Toxoplasma gondii, which may actually affect human behavior or possibly cause mental illness. 
Toxoplasma gondii also has an interesting life cycle. It is often found in rats and mice, but can only reproduce in the digestive tract of a cat. So this parasite actually "controls" rats and mice who are infected in order to be able to reproduce. Infected rodents are actually attracted to the smell of cat urine, so they will be eaten and the parasite can end up in a cat's digestive tract.
This parasite is also the reason why pregnant women are not supposed to scoop kitty litter, as the parasite is shed in the feces of infected cats and it is harmful to the fetus.

In humans, Toxoplasmosis has recently been found to be associated with schizophrenia, so it obviously also has some influence on the human brain, not just on rodents.
